summary: For ages 7–9: ice comes in different forms and water exists in three states. Learners investigate that dissolved salt lowers water's freezing point (seawater freezes below 0°C, near about -1.8°C) and classify polar ice by ORIGIN: sea ice (frozen ocean, salty, relatively thin) vs glacial ice (snow compacted over centuries on land, fresh, very thick) vs icebergs (chunks calved from glaciers, so fresh land-born ice). Water exists as solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (vapour), and ice/water are the same substance changing state. A hands-on fair test and sorting-by-origin tasks anchor these ideas, with a later qualitative hook to how melting floating sea ice vs land ice affects sea level differently.
misconceptions: All ice is the same — sea ice, glacial ice and icebergs differ in origin, saltiness and thickness
Seawater freezes at 0°C like fresh water — salt lowers the freezing point, so it freezes colder
Icebergs are frozen seawater — they calve from glaciers, so they are compacted snow and fresh, not salty
Ice and water are different substances — they are the same water in different states
Melting sea ice raises sea level a lot — floating sea ice barely changes it; land ice melting is what adds water

activities.title: Fair test: does salt change the temperature at which water freezes?
steps: Set up two samples: one fresh water, one salty water (e.g. with a measured spoon of salt stirred in).
Use the same amount of water, the same type of container and the same starting temperature, and place both in the same freezer/cold spot so the test is fair — only the salt differs.
Observe which freezes first, and if a thermometer is available, record the temperature at which each turns to ice.

Record what you actually observe. Fresh water normally freezes at about 0°C; salty water usually stays liquid longer and must get colder before it starts to freeze (with a lot of salt it may not freeze at all in a home freezer).
State the conclusion in your own words: salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes.
activities.insight: Dissolved salt lowers water's freezing point, so seawater must get colder than 0°C before it freezes — the two samples differ only because of the salt.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain with salt on ice
steps: Before touching anything, PREDICT and give a reason: will sprinkling salt on an ice cube make it warmer, colder, or do nothing?

Sprinkle salt on one ice cube and leave a second, unsalted cube beside it for comparison, then OBSERVE: compare how quickly each melts and, if possible, read a thermometer in each (the salted mixture can drop below 0°C while plain melting ice stays near 0°C), watch for frost on the outside of a metal cup, or touch the cup only briefly to feel it getting colder.
EXPLAIN what happened: salt lowers water's freezing point, which is why the salted ice-and-water mixture can sit below 0°C and why the sea must get colder than 0°C before it freezes.
Connect to everyday life: explain why people scatter salt on icy roads and paths in winter.
activities.insight: Salt lowers the freezing point; this is the same idea behind seawater freezing below 0°C and behind salting icy roads.

activities.title: Sort the three ices by where they came from
steps: Examine three ice examples (or labelled cards/cross-sections): frozen ocean water, compacted mountain-glacier snow, and an iceberg that snapped off a glacier.
For each, decide its ORIGIN (ocean vs land snow), whether it is salty or fresh, and whether it is thin or very thick.
Place the iceberg with the glacial/land-born group and explain why: it calved from a glacier, so it is compacted snow — fresh, not salty.
Build a short classification chart: sea ice = frozen ocean, salty, relatively thin; glacial ice = compacted snow on land, fresh, very thick; iceberg = broken-off glacier, fresh and usually thick.
State the key idea aloud: not all white ice is the same — it can come from the salty sea or from freshwater land snow.
activities.insight: Polar ice is distinguished by origin, not just appearance; this determines whether it is salty or fresh.

activities.title: The same water in three states
steps: Trace the state-change sequence: ice melts to water, water evaporates to vapour, and the reverse (vapour condenses, water freezes).
Explain that ice and liquid water are the same substance in different states, not different materials.
Connect the three states to the water cycle (evaporation, precipitation, meltwater).
Give one example of each state of water from everyday life.
activities.insight: Freezing and melting change water's state, not its identity; the same water can be solid, liquid or gas.

activities.title: Which melting ice changes the sea level? (foreshadowing)
steps: Compare two cases: a chunk of ice already floating in the sea, and ice sitting on land (a glacier).
Predict what happens to the water level when each melts.
Reason it through: floating sea ice already displaces its own water, so melting it barely changes the level; land ice adds new water to the sea when it melts.
State why this distinction matters when thinking about how melting ice affects the ocean.
activities.insight: Melting floating sea ice barely changes sea level, whereas melting land ice adds water and raises it.

checkQuestion: There are two kinds of ice near the poles: sea ice (frozen seawater) and glacial ice (from snow squashed down over centuries), and icebergs break off glaciers. A student says 'ice is just ice — it's all the same frozen water, and salty seawater freezes at the same temperature as fresh water.' Is all polar ice the same, and does salt water freeze at the same temperature as fresh? Explain the differences.
checkAnswer: No. Sea ice forms when the ocean freezes — it's relatively thin and comes from salty water; glacial ice forms from snow compressed over centuries on land — it's fresh water and very thick, and icebergs are chunks that break off glaciers and float out to sea. And salt water does NOT freeze at the same temperature as fresh: salt LOWERS the freezing point, so seawater must get colder than 0°C before it freezes. Water can also be solid (ice), liquid (water) or gas (water vapour).
